subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

periods.activity_title: Mystery Box: Who Is the Hidden Multiplier?

tasks_in_class.description: Guess the multiplier from four numbers coming out of the box; determine if more than one multiplier is possible; identify what numbers were put inside.
Make different arrays for 10, 14, 13, 20, 25, 32, 37, 46, 54 and identify the factors in each case.

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws a mystery box on the board with four numbers entering and four transformed numbers coming out. Students discuss what rule the box might be applying — Find the hidden numbers. (a)(b)(c), p.164 ("Guess the multiplier from four numbers coming out...."). Pairs share guesses and test whether a second multiplier could also work.

Students use squared paper or counters to build every possible rectangular arrangement for each number in Let Us Do (a)–(i), p.165 ("Make different arrays for 10, 14, 13, 20, 25, 32, 37, 46, 54...."). They record each arrangement as a multiplication sentence and list the factors they find. Numbers like 13 and 37 prompt the class to notice that only one non-trivial arrangement is possible, raising the question of what makes these numbers special.

Groups share their factor lists for 13 and 37. The teacher steers a whole-class discussion: what is it about these numbers that limits their arrays? Students articulate in their own words what it means for a number to have exactly two factors, consolidating the concept of prime numbers as an observation rather than a definition.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently assume that a larger number must have more factors; the arrays for 37 (only 1 × 37) often surprise them, and this moment is worth pausing on. Watch for students who list 1 and the number itself as an array without drawing it — insist they build it with counters so the concrete reality sticks. The common error is writing a factor pair only once (e.g., 2 × 5 but not 5 × 2) when both orientations of the array are distinct and worth recording.
materials: counters or tiles (at least 54 per pair)

section_titles: Common multiples via animal number-line jumps
periods.activity_title: Rabbit and Frog Race: Who Lands Together?

tasks_in_class.description: Rabbit jumps 4 each time, frog jumps 3; use the number line to find numbers both animals will touch — common multiples of 3 and 4.
Spider jumps 3 every time, grasshopper jumps 6; use the number line to find the common multiples of 3 and 6.
Find 5 common multiples for each of the following pairs: 2&3, 5&8, 2&4, 3&9, 5&10, 9&12, 8&12, 6&8, 6&9.

time_bands.activity: A large number line (0–30) is drawn on the board or laid on the floor. Two students act as rabbit (steps of 4) and frog (steps of 3), marking their landing squares with different colours — Animal Jumps, p.165 ("Rabbit jumps 4 each time, frog jumps 3; find numbers both touch...."). The class calls out which squares both animals land on and the teacher circles shared squares in a third colour.

The activity repeats with spider (steps of 3) and grasshopper (steps of 6) on the same number line — Animal Jumps (spider/grasshopper), p.166 ("Spider jumps 3 every time, grasshopper jumps 6; find common multiples...."). Students notice that every grasshopper landing is also a spider landing and discuss why this pattern appears.

Students work individually or in pairs on Let Us Do Q1 (a)–(h), p.166 ("Find 5 common multiples for pairs: 2&3, 5&8, 2&4...."). They list multiples for each number in a pair and circle the ones that appear in both lists. The teacher circulates, checking that students are using times-table sequences rather than guessing.

periods.teacher_notes: The spider-grasshopper pair is pivotal: when one jump size is a multiple of the other, every larger-jump landing is automatically a common multiple, and students who notice this early are ready to generalise. A frequent error is listing multiples that are only in one list; ask students to underline their two lists separately before circling matches. Pairs 9 & 12 and 6 & 8 tend to catch students who stop after finding two or three multiples — encourage them to extend their lists until five are confirmed.
materials: large number line strip (0–30) on board or floor
two colours of chalk or markers

section_titles: Common multiples via animal number-line jumps
periods.activity_title: Who Reaches the Food? Reasoning With Common Multiples

tasks_in_class.description: Robby rabbit jumps 4, Deeku deer jumps 6, both start at 0; will both reach the food at the end of the road? Who reaches first? Explain.
Mowgli jumps by 2 steps from 0 along a winding trail; identify which of his friends (at marked positions) he will be able to visit.

time_bands.activity: The teacher retells the Robby-rabbit and Deeku-deer scenario from Let Us Do Q2, p.167 ("Robby jumps 4, Deeku jumps 6; will both reach the food? Who first?"). Students predict independently, writing their guess and a one-sentence reason before any class discussion begins.

Students list multiples of 4 and 6 side by side on their paper and identify the common ones — Let Us Do Q2, p.167. They determine which common multiples both animals reach, then reason about which animal arrives first by comparing how many jumps each needs. Pairs share their reasoning and the class settles on a shared answer with justification.

Students work on Let Us Do Q3, p.167 ("Mowgli jumps by 2 steps; which friends can he visit?"). They mark multiples of 2 on the trail and identify which friends sit at those positions. The class discusses why some friends are skipped, connecting to the idea that a number must be in the multiples sequence to be reachable — solidifying what common multiples mean in a real navigation context.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse 'reaches first' with 'reaches a higher number first' — redirect them to count the number of jumps each animal needs to reach the same spot. The Mowgli trail question is well-suited to partner discussion: ask one student to mark the trail positions and the other to list multiples of 2, then compare. A common oversight is forgetting to check position 0; remind students that both animals start there.
materials: printed or drawn Mowgli winding trail (p.167)

section_titles: Common factors via jump model and divisibility
periods.activity_title: Mowgli's Trail in Reverse: Finding Jump Sizes That Fit

tasks_in_class.description: On Mowgli's trail, identify which friends he meets jumping by 3 steps; confirm 3 is a common factor of the positions landed on.
List all numbers Mowgli touches jumping by 5 steps; complete: '5 is a common factor of the numbers ___'.
Find common factors of 24 and 36 by testing jump sizes 2, 3, 4; find other jumps that reach both; list all common factors; check jump of 1.

time_bands.activity: Using the same Mowgli trail, the teacher asks: instead of Mowgli choosing his jump, the trail has friends at fixed positions — which jump size lands on all of them? Students work through Mowgli trail — jump by 3, p.168 ("Identify which friends Mowgli meets jumping by 3 steps...."), listing the positions and writing the multiplication sentence that shows 3 divides each one.

Students independently complete Mowgli trail — jump by 5, p.168 ("List numbers Mowgli touches jumping by 5; complete '5 is a common factor of ___'"). They compare the lists from jumps of 3 and 5 and notice which positions appear in both, beginning to articulate the idea of a shared factor.

Students investigate Let Us Do Q4 (a)–(f), p.168 ("Find common factors of 24 and 36 by testing jumps of 2, 3, 4; find others; list all; check jump of 1...."). They work systematically, testing each jump size and recording which ones divide both 24 and 36 exactly. The class shares results and the teacher helps students list all common factors in order, checking that jump of 1 is always included.

periods.teacher_notes: The shift from common multiples to common factors often confuses students: previously Mowgli chose his jump size freely; now the positions are fixed and the jump must fit them exactly. Emphasise this reversal explicitly. A frequent error at Q4 is stopping after finding factors 2, 3, and 4 and missing 6 and 12; prompt students to ask 'Have I tested every number up to the smaller of 24 and 36?' Also note Mowgli trail — jump by 10, p.168 (T-10) as additional practice if time permits.
materials: factor-testing recording sheet or squared paper

section_titles: Common factors via jump model and divisibility
periods.activity_title: Common Factors of Pairs: Listing and Checking

tasks_in_class.description: What are the common factors of 12 and 13?
From the numbers 0, 10, 16, 27, 36, 48 on a number line, find which can be reached by jumps of 4; complete '4 is the common factor of ___'.
Find the common factors of eight pairs: 12&16, 8&12, 4&16, 2&9, 3&5, 12&15, 20&5, 9&21, 6&27.

time_bands.activity: The teacher poses Let Us Do Q5, p.168 ("What are the common factors of 12 and 13?") as a think-pair task. Students list factors of 12 and factors of 13 separately, then look for shared entries. The result — only 1 — surprises many and leads to a discussion connecting back to the finding from the array work: 13 is prime, so its only factors are 1 and itself.

Students work through Let Us Do Q6, p.169 ("From 0, 10, 16, 27, 36, 48 find which are reached by jumps of 4; complete '4 is the common factor of ___'"). They test each number for divisibility by 4, cross out those that fail, and write the completion sentence with the remaining numbers.

Students tackle Let Us Do Q7 (a)–(h), p.169 ("Find the common factors of eight pairs: 12&16, 8&12, 4&16...."). They list factors of each number in a pair, circle the shared ones, and record the common-factor set. The teacher draws attention to pairs like 2 & 9 and 3 & 5 whose only common factor is 1, connecting these to the concept of co-prime numbers informally.

periods.teacher_notes: Q5 is a compact but rich task: the meeting of a composite number (12) and a prime number (13) with only the common factor 1 makes a memorable conceptual anchor. Students working on Q7 often miss factor 1 — insist they include it in every list. The pairs 2 & 9 and 3 & 5 are worth discussing whole-class because they preview the idea that some number pairs share no factor other than 1.

section_titles: Common factors via jump model and divisibility
periods.activity_title: True or False? Reasoning About Factors and Multiples

tasks_in_class.description: State True or False: factors of even numbers must be even; multiples of odd numbers cannot be even; factors of odd numbers cannot be even; one common multiple of two consecutive numbers is their product; the only common factor of consecutive numbers is 1; 0 cannot be a factor.
Sher Khan hunts every 3rd day, Bagheera every 5th day; if both start on the same day, on which days will they hunt together?
Mowgli wants to visit Baloo at position 30 but avoid Sher Khan at 25; how long (in steps) could each jump be?
What jump size lets Mowgli meet both Kaa at position 21 and Akela at position 35?

time_bands.activity: Students individually mark each statement in Let Us Do Q8 (a)–(f), p.169 ("State True or False: factors of even numbers must be even; multiples of odd numbers cannot be even....") as T or F and write a one-line counter-example or justification for each. Small groups of three compare answers and must reach agreement, citing a specific number to support any 'False' verdict.

The teacher reads out Let Us Do Q9, p.169 ("Sher Khan hunts every 3rd day, Bagheera every 5th day; on which days do they hunt together?"). Students list multiples of 3 and multiples of 5 in two columns and circle the shared entries, translating day numbers into a written answer.

Students solve Let Us Do Q10(a), p.169 ("Mowgli visits Baloo at 30, avoids Sher Khan at 25; what jump sizes work?") and Let Us Do Q10(b), p.169 ("Jump size to reach both Kaa at 21 and Akela at 35?"). They find factors of 30, check which do NOT divide 25, then find common factors of 21 and 35, writing their answers in complete sentences.

periods.teacher_notes: The True/False statements in Q8 are deliberately tricky; statement (a) — 'factors of even numbers must be even' — is False (4 has factor 1, which is odd) and consistently catches students. Encourage them to test the smallest possible even number before deciding. For Q10(b), students who confuse 'common factor' with 'common multiple' will list multiples of 21 and 35 instead; redirect them to the jump-size question: which size divides both 21 and 35 exactly?

periods.activity_title: Venn Diagram Sort: Divisible by 2, 5, or 10?

tasks_in_class.description: Sort 90, 45, 84, 22, 66, 56, 38, 78, 25, 30, 62, 95, 75, 40, 55 into a Venn diagram: divisible by 2 only, 5 only, 10 only, or 2 & 5 & 10.

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws three overlapping circles on the board labelled '÷2', '÷5', '÷10' and asks the class what they notice about numbers that end in 0 — which circles would they belong to and why? Students offer examples and the class builds the divisibility rules for 2, 5, and 10 together through observation before any formal statement is made.

Students work through Let Us Do Q11 (a)–(d), p.170 ("Sort 90, 45, 84, 22, 66, 56, 38, 78, 25, 30, 62, 95, 75, 40, 55 into a Venn diagram...."). They test each number using the last-digit rules and place it in the correct region of their drawn Venn diagram. Pairs check each other's placements.

The class builds a shared Venn diagram on the board, with students taking turns placing numbers. The teacher probes: 'Can a number be in the ÷5 circle but not the ÷2 circle? Can it be in ÷2 and ÷10 but not ÷5? What would have to be true?' This reasoning cements why the three circles overlap in the way they do and consolidates the relationship among divisibility by 2, 5, and 10.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often place numbers ending in 0 only in the ÷10 region, forgetting these numbers are also divisible by 2 and 5 and belong in the intersection of all three circles. The discussion question — 'Can a number be in ÷2 and ÷10 but not ÷5?' — is a useful diagnostic; the answer is No, and working out why consolidates the rule. Numbers like 84 and 22 that are divisible by 2 only sometimes get incorrectly placed in the centre intersection; ask students to verify by attempting division by 5.
materials: Venn diagram worksheet or blank paper for drawing three overlapping circles
the list of 15 numbers from Q11 (written on board or in worksheet)

section_titles: Common multiples via animal number-line jumps
Common factors via jump model and divisibility
periods.activity_title: Bringing It All Together: Factors, Multiples and the Jumps Between

time_bands.activity: The teacher places six numbers on the board — 12, 15, 24, 30, 36, 60 — and asks students to quickly build a factor list for each in their notebooks. When lists are ready, the class pools them and discusses: which of these numbers share the most factors? Which share none beyond 1? This activates the array-based understanding of factors and reconnects to the prime-number finding from the finding-factors-using-arrays work.

In pairs, students choose any two numbers from the set and list five common multiples and all common factors of that pair. They then circle every common multiple that is also divisible by 10, using the last-digit rule to check quickly. Each pair writes one sentence: 'The common factors of ___ and ___ are ___, and five common multiples are ___.' Pairs share and compare, noticing how different choices of number pairs affect the size and number of common factors and common multiples.

The teacher poses a new synthesis problem: 'Two animals jump along a number line — one in steps of 6, the other in steps of 9. Will they ever land on 54? Will they ever land on 25? Explain your answer using both multiples and divisibility.' Students work individually, listing multiples of 6 and 9, checking divisibility by 10 where relevant, and writing a short explanation. This mirrors the animal-jumps context that runs through common multiples via animal number-line jumps and common factors via jump model and divisibility.

A quick whole-class round: the teacher calls out a number and students call out one fact about it — a factor, a multiple, a divisibility rule, or a prime observation. The teacher collects responses on the board, weaving them into a short spoken map of the chapter's ideas: arrays show factors, number-line jumps show multiples, shared jump sizes are common factors, and last-digit shortcuts tell us divisibility by 2, 5, and 10.

periods.teacher_notes: The synthesis problem with jumps of 6 and 9 is designed to require students to reach across all four strands: listing multiples (common multiples work), testing divisibility (divisibility-rules work), and reasoning about which jump size reaches a given position (common factors work). Students who conflate factors and multiples — a persistent confusion across the chapter — will struggle with 'Will they land on 25?' because 25 is not a multiple of either 6 or 9; use this as a diagnostic conversation point. Avoid accepting answers that list correct numbers without explanation; the explanatory sentence is the evidence of connected understanding.

items.section_title: Common multiples via animal number-line jumps
items.prompt: A cat jumps 4 steps at a time and a dog jumps 5 steps at a time. Both start at 0 on a number line. List the first three numbers where both animals land.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: List multiples of 4 and multiples of 5 separately, then identify numbers that appear in both lists.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student colour-mark cat jumps and dog jumps in two colours on the number line. Stretch: find the fourth and fifth common landing spots.

exercise.description: Rabbit jumps 4 each time, frog jumps 3; use the number line to find numbers both animals will touch — common multiples of 3 and 4.

items.section_title: Common multiples via animal number-line jumps
items.prompt: A beetle jumps 4 steps each time and an ant jumps 8 steps each time. Both start at 0. Which of the following is true about their landing spots?

options.label: A
options.text: Every ant landing is also a beetle landing.

options.label: B
options.text: Every beetle landing is also an ant landing.

options.label: C
options.text: The animals first land together at 32.

options.label: D
options.text: The two animals never land on the same spot.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Every ant landing is also a beetle landing.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: List multiples of 4 and multiples of 8; observe that 8 is itself a multiple of 4, so every multiple of 8 is also a multiple of 4.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has reversed the relationship: beetle jumps are smaller, so beetle lands more often, not less.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has not listed multiples and does not see that 8, 16, 24, … are also multiples of 4.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may be thinking of a different pair; the first shared landing is 8, not 32.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student mark beetle jumps and ant jumps on a number line up to 32 in two colours. Stretch: change ant's jump to 6 and ask whether the same pattern holds.

exercise.description: Spider jumps 3 every time, grasshopper jumps 6; use the number line to find the common multiples of 3 and 6.

items.prompt: A mystery box multiplies every number put in by the same hidden number. When 5 goes in, 35 comes out. When 8 goes in, 56 comes out. What is the hidden multiplier? Can there be a different hidden multiplier that fits both outputs? Explain.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The hidden multiplier is 7. There is no other multiplier, because 35 ÷ 5 = 7 and 56 ÷ 8 = 7, and both divisions give the same unique answer.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide each output by its input; if both quotients match, that quotient is the unique multiplier.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to try each number from 1 to 10 as the multiplier and check both outputs. Stretch: invent a new input-output pair that fits the same box, and one that does not.

exercise.description: Guess the multiplier from four numbers coming out of the box; determine if more than one multiplier is possible; identify what numbers were put inside.

items.prompt: Priya tries to arrange 17 tiles into a rectangular array with more than one row and more than one column. How many such arrangements can she make?

options.label: C
options.text: None — 17 cannot be arranged that way.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: None — 17 is a prime number, so its only factors are 1 and 17, and neither gives a rectangle with more than one row and more than one column.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: List factor pairs of 17; only 1 × 17 is possible, meaning no arrangement with both dimensions greater than 1 exists.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may be thinking of the 1 × 17 arrangement and not applying the 'more than one row and column' condition.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may be confusing 17 with a number like 15, which has arrangements 3 × 5 and 5 × 3.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student likely guessed without checking factor pairs.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student physically try to arrange 17 counters into equal rows of 2, 3, 4, … and count leftovers. Stretch: list all numbers from 10 to 20 that share the same property as 17.

exercise.description: Make different arrays for 10, 14, 13, 20, 25, 32, 37, 46, 54 and identify the factors in each case.

items.section_title: Common multiples via animal number-line jumps
items.prompt: Rajan jumps 4 steps at a time and Sunil jumps 6 steps at a time, both starting at 0. There is food at position 24. Will both reach position 24? Who gets there in fewer jumps? Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes, both reach 24. Rajan takes 6 jumps (4 × 6 = 24); Sunil takes 4 jumps (6 × 4 = 24). Sunil gets there in fewer jumps.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check whether 24 is a multiple of each jump size, then divide 24 by each jump size to count jumps needed.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: list multiples of 4 and multiples of 6 in two columns and ask the student to look for 24 in each. Stretch: find the next position beyond 24 where both would land together.

exercise.description: Robby rabbit jumps 4, Deeku deer jumps 6, both start at 0; will both reach the food at the end of the road? Who reaches first? Explain.

items.section_title: Common factors via jump model and divisibility
items.prompt: List all factors of 18 and all factors of 24. Then write down every number that appears in both lists. What is the largest number in your shared list?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. Factors of 24: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24. Common factors: 1, 2, 3, 6. The largest common factor is 6.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: List all factor pairs for each number, then circle those that appear in both lists; the largest circled number is the answer.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: use counters to build all rectangular arrays for 18 and then for 24 before listing factors. Stretch: find the common factors of 18, 24, and 36 all at once.

exercise.description: Find common factors of 24 and 36 by testing jump sizes 2, 3, 4; find other jumps that reach both; list all common factors; check jump of 1.

items.section_title: Common factors via jump model and divisibility
items.prompt: Which of the following statements is TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: 0 can be a factor of any number.

options.label: B
options.text: All factors of an even number must also be even.

options.label: C
options.text: Multiples of an odd number can never be even.

options.label: D
options.text: The only common factor of two consecutive numbers is 1.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The only common factor of two consecutive numbers is 1.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Test each statement with a small example: consecutive numbers like 8 and 9 share no factor other than 1; 6 has factor 3 which is odd; 3 × 2 = 6 which is even; division by 0 is undefined.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has not tested: 6 has odd factor 3, so factors of an even number need not all be even.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has confused odd numbers with their multiples; 3 is odd but 3 × 2 = 6 is even.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student does not know that division by 0 is undefined and that 0 cannot divide any number.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to test statement B with the specific pair 7 and 8, listing all factors of each. Stretch: write their own True statement about factors or multiples and give a number example to back it up.

exercise.description: State True or False: factors of even numbers must be even; multiples of odd numbers cannot be even; factors of odd numbers cannot be even; one common multiple of two consecutive numbers is their product; the only common factor of consecutive numbers is 1; 0 cannot be a factor.

items.prompt: Neha says: 'If a number is divisible by 10, it must also be divisible by both 2 and 5.' Is she right?

options.label: A
options.text: No — a number can be divisible by 10 without being divisible by 5.

options.label: B
options.text: No — divisible by 10 means only the last digit is 0, which says nothing about 2 or 5.

options.label: C
options.text: Only sometimes — it depends on whether the number is odd or even.

options.label: D
options.text: Yes — any number ending in 0 ends in an even digit and in 0 or 5.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes — any number divisible by 10 ends in 0, which is an even digit (so divisible by 2) and ends in 0 (so divisible by 5).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the last-digit divisibility rules: last digit 0 satisfies the rule for 2 (even last digit) and the rule for 5 (last digit 0 or 5) simultaneously.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has not connected the last-digit-0 rule to the separate rules for 2 and 5.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student is confusing the number itself being odd/even with the divisibility rules for 2 and 5.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student does not know that 5 is a factor of 10, so every multiple of 10 is automatically a multiple of 5.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to test three numbers ending in 0 (such as 20, 50, 70) by dividing each by 2, 5, and 10 in turn. Stretch: find a number divisible by 2 and 5 that is NOT divisible by 10, and explain why.

exercise.description: Sort 90, 45, 84, 22, 66, 56, 38, 78, 25, 30, 62, 95, 75, 40, 55 into a Venn diagram: divisible by 2 only, 5 only, 10 only, or 2 & 5 & 10.

items.section_title: Common multiples via animal number-line jumps
items.prompt: Which of the following is a common multiple of 3 and 8?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 24. It is a multiple of 3 (3 × 8 = 24) and a multiple of 8 (8 × 3 = 24).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check each option: divide by 3 and by 8; only the number that divides evenly by both is a common multiple.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student recognises 18 as a multiple of 3 but has not checked divisibility by 8.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student recognises 27 as a multiple of 3 but has not checked divisibility by 8.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student recognises 32 as a multiple of 8 but has not checked divisibility by 3.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: list the first ten multiples of 3 and the first ten multiples of 8 side by side and look for a shared number. Stretch: find the next two common multiples of 3 and 8 after 24.

exercise.description: Find 5 common multiples for each of the following pairs: 2&3, 5&8, 2&4, 3&9, 5&10, 9&12, 8&12, 6&8, 6&9.

items.section_title: Common factors via jump model and divisibility
items.prompt: What are the common factors of 12 and 18?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 1, 2, 3, 6. Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. Numbers in both lists: 1, 2, 3, 6.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: List all factors of each number, then identify those appearing in both lists.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has included 4, which is a factor of 12 but not of 18.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has included 9, which is a factor of 18 but not of 12.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has omitted 1, which is always a common factor of any two positive integers.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to write the full factor list for 12 and for 18 separately before comparing. Stretch: add a third number — say 24 — and find common factors of all three.

exercise.description: Find the common factors of eight pairs: 12&16, 8&12, 4&16, 2&9, 3&5, 12&15, 20&5, 9&21, 6&27.

items.section_title: Common factors via jump model and divisibility
items.prompt: A lion patrols the forest every 4 days and a leopard every 6 days. Both begin patrolling on day 1. On which day will they first patrol together again after day 1?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Day 13. Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16 … Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18 … The first common multiple after 0 is 12, so they patrol together again on day 1 + 12 = day 13.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: List multiples of 4 and multiples of 6; the smallest shared multiple is the number of days until they next coincide; add 1 because they started on day 1.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: list multiples of 4 and multiples of 6 up to 24 in two columns and circle the first shared number. Stretch: find the second day after day 1 when they patrol together.

exercise.description: Sher Khan hunts every 3rd day, Bagheera every 5th day; if both start on the same day, on which days will they hunt together?

items.section_title: Common factors via jump model and divisibility
items.prompt: Mowgli wants to visit a friend at position 28 and another friend at position 42 along a trail. He must jump the same number of steps each time and land exactly on both positions. What is the largest jump size that lets him do this?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 7. Factors of 28: 1, 2, 4, 7, 14, 28. Factors of 42: 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 14, 21, 42. Common factors: 1, 2, 7, 14. The largest is 14. Wait — verify: 28 ÷ 14 = 2 ✓; 42 ÷ 14 = 3 ✓. The largest jump size is 14.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: List all factors of 28 and all factors of 42; the largest number appearing in both lists is the answer.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: start by testing jump sizes 1, 2, 3, 4 in order and checking whether each divides both 28 and 42 exactly. Stretch: verify that a jump of 14 really lands on both 28 and 42 by writing the multiplication sentences, then find the next smaller jump size that also works.

exercise.description: What jump size lets Mowgli meet both Kaa at position 21 and Akela at position 35?
